items.title: What’s new in PHP 8.6 and what that means for WordPress?
items.desc: Having a reputation for long backward compatibility, as stable as it sounds, has an ugly face of dragging performance and security down, as well as keeping the shiny new functionalities away from WordPress core developers. Which PHP 8.6 features we can look forward to?
items.full: The new version of PHP, 8.6 , is set to be released on November 19th, just 2 days after WordPress 7.2 RC1 (release candidate 1). When we talk about PHP in relation to WordPress, we usually talk about the minimum version supported by core and plugins, which is, since WordPress 7.0, PHP 7.4 . The most talked-about new feature is partial function application (PFA), and rightfully so. With placeholders such as ? converting every parameter into required, and … keeping the original statuses and default values, it almost feels like magic. This will have a great impact on the pipe operator (|>), added in PHP 8.5 . Unfortunately, we won’t see any of these in WordPress core any time soon, as long as we don’t move minimum supported PHP versions more closely to more recently released PHP code. Another useful change in PHP 8.6 is the addition of the clamp() function, which frankly already exists in many frameworks. In WordPress, we saw the benefits of this logic in the 6.1 release when fluid typography entered the core . Even though fluid typography is a CSS enhancement, the clamp() function in PHP works basically the same: there’s a value and a defined range of minimum and maximum bounds for the returned value. While in CSS it is very useful for various numeric values, in PHP it can have broader applications, one of which is the range of dates. But rather than listing all the changes in the new PHP release, which you can already find in several places (I’ll link to them at the end of this article), I’d like to take the opportunity to look at this progress through WordPress’s eyes. Looking at WordPress’s relation to PHP 8.6, compatibility and feature adoption are two separate questions. On the compatibility side, WordPress is already actively working on it. PHP 8.6 is added to the PHPUnit matrix for the 7.2 development cycle, but the job is still allowed to fail. What we can expect are mostly deprecation notices, and mostly in tests. The list of deprecations in 8.6 , proposed for removal in PHP 9, is a long one, and WordPress core, as well as extenders, should carefully search through the code to locate them all. For example, PHP 8.6 is deprecating Oniguruma-based mbstring regex functionality . If you use mb_ereg() , mb_ereg_replace() , mb_split() , etc., you should follow the core example and start replacing them with modern counterparts. Another problem that core is already fixing is incorrectly-cased function calls that do not match their declaration. Other deprecations that need auditing include: As it seems, for compatibility needs, PHP 8.6 will make us look most closely at the following components: Let’s stop for a moment and imagine a world in which WordPress can start using new PHP features right away. My first heartbeat goes to URI/URL processing. Even though PHP introduced the URI extension in 8.5 , 8.6 adds 2 new classes and more functionality. WordPress core has an enormous amount of URL-handling code ( wp_parse_url() , home_url() , site_url() , admin_url() , esc_url() , etc.), plus URL handling through HTTP, REST, canonical redirects, multisite, block parsing, media, etc. Our lives would be much easier if we used the native PHP functionality

items.title: When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next?
items.desc: It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is 🫩 and that says a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the … When Everything Has Changed, What Do We Do Next? originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. It’s been a… year, huh? I think the most common emoji I’ve seen this year is 🫩 and that says a lot. One thing is for sure: the industry we make a living in is in flux, regardless of the outcomes of the AI bubble. Let’s take a look at how we can try and navigate that situation as best we can. But first… The reality of where we currently are Technology hyperscalers like Microsoft and Meta, along with AI startups like Open AI and Anthropic have transformed everything about tech and the job we do. This is true regardless of if they fail or somehow succeed in their quest to have everyone paying a subscription fee for their Large Language Model (LLM) technology, which is marketed to us as AI . I’ll refer to this technology as AI for the rest of this article for simplicity. It’s not just tech jobs that have transformed either. Everywhere you go, you will see some slop , somewhere. Be it a flyer, website, a village poster or a food truck menu. Heck, people are even using LLMs to work out what’s special about their own children . The effects of this technology are far-reaching, way beyond our own industry. The technology has hit us all in tech especially hard though. Mid-last year, I did some investigating because I suspected that so-called AI mandates were becoming increasingly popular and what I learned from conversations then feels like some sort of utopia compared to now . In the space between that piece being published and now , we went from token maxxing to companies realizing that actually, this technology is extremely expensive and not returning the promised outcomes . The mandates have cooled, sure, but the demands to use AI to produce more volume , regardless of whether that volume is actually needed or not are still very much there. I’m in a fortunate position to have friendships with people all across the industry, from tech hyperscalers, to tiny little studios, and the stories I have heard from their work life are nothing short of horrifying. No one really seems to be happy with their work either. This is such a long way away from even a handful of years ago where yes, there was a lot of problematic culture and outcomes from the tech industry, but people were generally quite happy with the work they were doing at least. The symptoms of where we currently are The sudden urge to sprint towards AI technologies over the last few years has had a devastating effect in so many places. The technology has encouraged suicide , devastated communities with the data center build-out and of course, displaced thousands of people’s careers . It’s worth noting that I’ve mentioned only a tiny sample of the harms there. If I listed them all, this article would be unbearably long and depressing. Some harms I do want to touch on though are the effects on our communities in tech. The community spirit of open source and open knowledge was the foundation of the industry’s — especially the web industry’s — rapid success. At the root of everything there was people happy to share knowledge and build everyone up with them . Those people still do exist — myself included — but being one of those people is

items.title: Mistral plays catch-up with Vibe Desktop as rivals already command full operating systems
items.desc: Mistral's AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app. The article Mistral plays catch-up with Vibe Desktop as rivals already command full operating systems appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Mistral's AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app. Mistral says users can give Vibe ( formerly "Le Chat" ) multiple tasks at once through the new desktop app and watch the agent work on them in parallel. Until now, Mistral only offered Vibe as a web app, a command-line tool, or a smartphone app. The desktop version ties together the local features of Vibe CLI with the cloud sessions from Vibe Code Web. The agent can work either in a local repository or in a cloud sandbox, and the app uses Git worktrees to keep parallel tasks in the same project separate. Beyond code, the Work mode now also has access to local files, though Mistral doesn't mention any computer-use capabilities. Competitors are further along. Anthropic's desktop app already lets Claude open apps, control browsers, and fill out spreadsheets since this spring. Mistral caught up on the model side in October with Large 4 , but in head-to-head comparisons it still trails Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 by a wide margin and also falls behind the strongest open models from China. The French company makes most of its money from enterprises and government agencies that run its models via API or on-premise. Ad Vibe Desktop is available for macOS and Windows from Mistral , with a Linux version planned. items.full: After years of uncertainty under corporate ownership, CSS-Tricks has a new chapter and a new owner. Geoff Graham joins Matt Medeiros to talk about bringing the beloved web development resource back to its community roots and building a sustainable future for the site. Geoff shares how DigitalOcean made the transition possible, why he wants CSS-Tricks… After years of uncertainty under corporate ownership, CSS-Tricks has a new chapter and a new owner. Geoff Graham joins Matt Medeiros to talk about bringing the beloved web development resource back to its community roots and building a sustainable future for the site. Geoff shares how DigitalOcean made the transition possible, why he wants CSS-Tricks to become a learning community rather than just another content site , and how memberships, sponsorships, and new educational opportunities will help support it. The conversation also gets into the bigger questions facing WordPress: Is AI making WordPress less necessary? Does the platform need a lighter version for simpler sites? And as AI changes how developers work, why will human expertise, education, and community matter even more? Plus, Geoff explains why CSS-Tricks is embracing multiple revenue streams, experimenting with cohort-based learning, and focusing on engagement over page views. New articles and episodes, plus the week’s WordPress news. A five-minute read. Free.

items.title: Discover 2WayMicropay: Sell WordPress Content From One Cent and Give Readers Credits to Spend
items.desc: Most readers won't subscribe for one article, and most micropayment systems still ask them to fund a wallet first. 2WayMicropay lets WordPress publishers charge from one cent and hand readers credits to spend on that content. The post " Discover 2WayMicropay: Sell WordPress Content From One Cent and Give Readers Credits to Spend " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: A visitor lands on one of your best articles from search, reads the opening, and hits a subscription wall. They wanted that one piece, not a monthly plan, so they leave, even though they’d probably have paid a dollar for it. Micropayments were supposed to close that gap, but most systems still ask a stranger to sign up and fund a wallet before they’ve read anything worth paying for. 2WayMicropay , from Qixit, removes that step by letting publishers charge from one cent and also hand readers credits to spend. The quickest way to see what’s different is to go through the flow as a reader. Qixit’s interactive paywall demo has you create a free Qixit consumer account, receive complimentary credits, and spend them to unlock premium articles about how 2WayMicropay works. Notice the order of events. You’re asked for an account, but never for a deposit, because the credits you spend arrive through the same system that charges for the content. Qixit is the company and account platform, and 2WayMicropay is its two-way micropayment product. The 2WayMicropay WordPress plugin lets visitors pay for posts, pages, comments, video, audio, downloads and other content in Qix Credits, at prices from one cent up to several dollars. The “two-way” part is what sets it apart. Most payment systems only move value from customer to seller, while 2WayMicropay also lets publishers, advertisers and sponsors send credits to visitors, which readers can then spend on content from participating publishers. It’s worth knowing that Qix Credits are platform credits. Qixit is clear that they aren’t cash or legal tender, and that redemption and withdrawal follow its own agreements and policies. You don’t have to drop subscriptions, memberships or ads to use it. 2WayMicropay sits beside them as an à-la-carte option for the readers a subscription wall turns away. Our guide to ways to monetize WordPress covers how the other models fit together. Checkout is hosted by Qixit, so there’s nothing for you to build. A visitor signs in or creates a free Qixit account, confirms the purchase, and gets access once payment goes through. The plugin is also a showcase for a broader platform. Qixit’s vendor tools and developer API let teams add the same purchase and payout links to custom websites and other applications. Each premium item gets an access rule: pay once and view forever, pay per view, limited hours, or session only. For a free preview, you add a WordPress “More” break and enable “Use Pay-per-play works the same way for video, audio and games through a product shortcode. That lets podcasters and video creators charge for a single episode on their own site. Payout links are created in Qixit’s vendor portal and added to posts with a shortcode or URL. For each one you set the amount, the credit type, a destination URL, a total budget and an optional expiry date. Qix Credits work across participating sites, while site-specific promotional credits can only be spent on your content, which gives readers a reason to come back. Either type can fund free trials or reward readers for viewing a sponsor’s page, completing a survey or referring a friend. You don’t need to open each post to monetize

items.title: AI agents are starting to fill out medical forms and file insurance requests in place of human staff
items.desc: OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to automate administrative tasks in US healthcare through computer-use agents that operate existing clinic software and insurance portals the way a human would. Luna handles tasks like prior authorizations for about 8.5 cents each. Companies including CVS Health and Cigna Healthcare are already deploying the technology. The article AI agents are starting to fill out medical forms and file insurance requests in place of human staff appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI wants GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6 Luna to click and type their way through clinic software and insurance portals as digital clerks. GPT-6 Luna handles administrative tasks for about 8.5 cents per task, according to the company. In a recent product announcement , OpenAI targets the lack of APIs in healthcare. The computer-use agents integrated into the Agents API in late September operate existing user interfaces the way a human would. In this case, they transfer data between electronic health records and external web portals. According to OpenAI, when a patient reports back pain, the agent is meant to search relevant prior findings and draft both an MRI order and a reply to the patient. It should also prepare a prior authorization request on the insurer's portal. Clinicians and the responsible administrative staff review these drafts before they are released. The features are available through the API as well as in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians. Ad In an evaluation described by OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra worked through tasks from electronic health record inboxes, among other things preparing an ibuprofen dosage for a child with a broken arm. Physician reviewers rated 99 percent of the 325 tasks evaluated as clinically safe. In 93 percent of 646 reviews, the reviewers called the prep work very or extremely helpful. For administrative workflows such as prior authorizations, appeals, or medical equipment orders, OpenAI points to the independent HealthAdminBench benchmark from Stanford University researchers . GPT-6 Astra scored 94.3 percent of possible points. GPT-6 Luna, built for low API pricing , scored 91.8 percent and, according to OpenAI, cost about 8.5 cents per task, 98 percent less than Astra. Both models ran at maximum reasoning effort on the benchmark. Ad Several partner organizations are helping advance the technology. At CVS Health, the agents already process referrals and specialist consultations across separate systems. According to the announcement, one agent cleared a months-long backlog of outgoing documents in one weekend, while another handles the system steps for tens of thousands of consultations daily. CVS Health published its software architecture as Agent Kit on GitHub. At insurer Cigna Healthcare, the models merge patient information from more than 10 separate systems. Abridge is developing the agents for planned use in clinical discharge planning. Ambience has demonstrated additional safety mechanisms in which an agent stops when a patient's record is unclear and asks a physician for input. Startups like Assort also use the feature in Codex to complete referrals in practice management software whose APIs don't support that final click. Ad Because the agents work directly in electronic health records, protecting sensitive health data is a core concern. OpenAI says it does not use organizational data to train its base models. ChatGPT for Healthcare offers role-based access controls and audit logs, according to the company. Organizations can also configure the applications and environments so an agent only accesses the records and actions needed for a given task. Ad For HIPAA-compliant workflows with protect

items.title: The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output
items.desc: The US is tightening its chip export controls. Data centers in third countries like Singapore and Malaysia will soon need a US license to buy Nvidia chips, closing the loophole that let Chinese firms rent cloud compute abroad. A Reuters investigation also reveals how China offsets its hardware shortage through industrial-scale distillation of US AI models. The article The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The US wants to block China from renting AI power abroad but China already built a parallel supply chain from US AI output Maximilian Schreiner View the LinkedIn Profile of Maximilian Schreiner Nov 17, 2026 Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Chinese companies have been skirting US export bans by legally renting Nvidia computing power in third countries. After Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, the US is closing that loophole. An investigation also reveals how China has cushioned the years-long chip embargo through an entire industry built around model distillation. For years, the US has tried to cut China off from importing advanced AI processors through strict export controls. Chinese companies responded by exploiting an entirely legal loophole, renting the computing power they needed through cloud-based remote access from foreign data centers that were allowed to receive US hardware. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) at the US Commerce Department now wants to shut down that workaround with an interim rule . It aligns remote-access rules with existing physical export bans. Data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil will need a US government license to buy advanced AI chips from US manufacturers like Nvidia, Bloomberg reports . Applications will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Subsidiaries of US-headquartered companies are exempt from the license requirement, as are shipments to data centers running only commercial recommendation systems for online retailers or social media platforms. The rules take effect once published in the Federal Register. Nvidia's stock fell as much as 2.9 percent after the announcement, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped up to 5.5 percent. The political trigger, though, was suspected illegal smuggling of physical chips. The new rule comes just days after the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who had admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former manager at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. US authorities suspect Alice Huang, who now lives in China, of espionage. They are investigating Megaspeed for possible export-control violations after banned Nvidia chips reportedly turned up in a Chinese data center linked to her. Megaspeed denies any wrongdoing, and President Donald Trump said Monday that Jensen Huang did not compromise national security. The scandal still set off an open power struggle in Washington over lax enforcement of chip sanctions. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had delayed a Trump-authorized measure against illegal chip diversions, according to Axios, prompting Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to publicly accuse him of inaction. The Commerce Department's announcement now states with unusual bluntness that the draft rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. A separate exclusive Reuters investigation shows how Chinese developers cope with the years-long shortage of top-tier domestic hardware. items.full: OpenAI is giving NATO and several European governments access to its cybersecurity tool Daybreak. Through Daybreak , cyber defense teams can use OpenAI's models to audit software, find vulnerabilities, and patch security gaps. The NATO Communications and Information Agency (NCIA) says it's already using the underlying models heavily. NCIA chief Dylan Browne called it a generational leap in cyber defense. During the NATO exercise Crossed Swords 2026 , participants deployed AI agents for cyber operations under human oversight for the first time. The models have already delivered results elsewhere. The EU's cybersecurity agency ENISA used them to find four vulnerabilities in software used by EU institutions. A joint report with CERT-EU examined 27 software projects, and 95 percent of the 88 reported issues turned out to be real bugs. Poland's CERT Polska found six vulnerabilities in MikroTik routers that were being actively exploited. Ukraine is using Daybreak to protect civilian infrastructure. France, Germany, and Poland have also been granted access. items.title: Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years
items.desc: Edinburgh's Childlight Institute reports a more than 8,400 percent increase in AI-generated child sexual abuse material over two years, from about 4,700 reports in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025. Abusers are using tools like nudify apps for blackmail. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency. The article Reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material have surged more than 8,400 percent in two years appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Reports of AI being used for the sexual exploitation of children have jumped more than 8,400 percent in two years. According to a report by Edinburgh's Childlight Institute, the number of reported AI-generated abuse images climbed from about 4,700 in 2023 to over 400,000 in 2025, The Guardian reports . The material includes AI-manipulated images (deepfakes) from so-called "nudify apps" that digitally strip people of their clothing. Abusers can use the faked images to blackmail children into handing over money or more photos. The data comes from reports that tech companies filed with the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC). The UK's Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) reviewed 6,310 criminal, photorealistic AI-generated abuse images in the first half of 2026 alone. That's 40 percent more than in all of 2025. Childlight data director Debi Fry acknowledges that better detection systems partly explain the spike. She still calls for swift action from lawmakers and tech companies. Childlight CEO Paul Stanfield wants governments to classify the problem as a preventable public health emergency, dedicate funding to prevention, and coordinate efforts across healthcare, schools, child protection services, and the justice system. items.title: Why operational visibility is becoming more valuable than performance scores
items.desc: Your client’s WooCommerce homepage scores 98 in Lighthouse. They’re happy with that, until a customer emails: “I enter my delivery address, and checkout just sits there.” ...
items.full: Your client’s WooCommerce homepage scores 98 in Lighthouse. They’re happy with that, until a customer emails: “I enter my delivery address, and checkout just sits there.” You try it yourself. Everything works. By the following afternoon, another complaint arrives. The homepage still loads quickly, and another speed test gives you little to investigate. Somewhere in the live site, under conditions your test doesn’t reproduce, customers struggle to place an order. Performance reports are more than just a simple score, though. Your team needs to know what runs during the slowdown and where requests spend their time. Otherwise, troubleshooting becomes a sequence of guesses, each with its own chance of disrupting the store. As sites take on more automated work, those questions become harder to answer from the browser alone. This article follows that checkout problem from the first complaint through the fix, with a look at the evidence your agency needs and how to explain the results to a client. A Lighthouse report earns its place in a developer’s toolkit. It can expose a large image that delays the main content or JavaScript that keeps the browser busy. Fixing those problems improves the experience people have on the page. The performance score combines several measurements from the test. It’s useful for comparing changes under similar conditions, provided you pay attention to the individual metrics behind it. The trouble starts when a client reads “98” as confirmation that everything on the website works well. A standard homepage audit doesn’t usually involve filling a cart and submitting a shipping address. It doesn’t wait for the afternoon inventory update, either. Instead, it measures the page you ask it to test, under the conditions of that run. PageSpeed Insights also includes field data from the Chrome User Experience Report when enough data is available. That reflects real visitors over a rolling 28-day period. The Lighthouse score comes from a separate lab test. Mixing those up makes the report harder to explain. Real-user Core Web Vitals give you a broader view of page experience. They still don’t identify which function inside an import plugin puts pressure on the database. For the store in our example, the homepage score can be entirely legitimate. A cached page reaches visitors quickly while checkout waits on work inside WordPress. The useful question is whether your measurements cover the interaction customers complain about. A fast homepage tells you something worth knowing. It leaves plenty of the store untested. At 2 p.m., the store imports a supplier’s stock file. Nobody opens the WordPress dashboard to start it. A scheduled task begins processing product records while customers continue shopping. That import needs database time. Depending on how the plugin runs it, it also occupies PHP threads that serve other requests. Moving work into the background changes when it happens, but the work still uses resources. WordPress cron jobs and queue runners can make this activity easy to overlook. The schedule lives in a plugin setting, and the person who configures it may have no reason to revisit it until something slows down. AI agent

items.full: About The Author Juggling between three languages on a daily basis, Iris is known for her love of linguistics, arts, web design and typography, as well as her goldmine of … More about Iris ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. AI is changing how we design and build, and it isn’t slowing down. On December 1, 2026, SmashingConf is hosting the AI 2027 Conference , a live online half day event to take stock of where AI stands today, what we can expect in 2027, and where teams are getting it right. With AI maturing, it’s clear we need to learn how AI can elevate your workflow as a UX designer and Design System engineer. Most of us are still figuring it out and trying to work smarter in this new world, so we invited industry experts who have been doing this for a while. They show their experience and tell you what works and what doesn’t , so you don’t have to figure it all out yourself. Every session is practical. Speakers show how they actually work: their tools, their setups, and the small things that are easy to miss. items.title: AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?
items.desc: AI has sped up how teams design and build, but quality assurance (QA) testing hasn’t kept pace, and the web may be getting less accessible. Drawing on new research, Andrew Chung explains what separates the teams whose accessibility efforts are keeping up, and how to embed human judgment into AI-enabled workflows without slowing delivery.
items.full: About The Author Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access , a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬ Weekly tips on front-end & UX . Trusted by 182,000+ folks. This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access , who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you! Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report . Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up. We asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage. These results point to a two-speed workflow . AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible? Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now. This matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor. So how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace? We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently. Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge shows up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training , communication , and a culture of accessibility . A quick caveat : This is survey data, so it only shows correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore. And it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize issues. items.full: I've been leaning hard into Claude Fable 5.2 to help knock things off the 1.0 milestone , which is now 53% complete. The biggest 1.0 item in this release is streaming support for output renderers - the built-in TSV and CSV export mechanisms now use this as well, and plugins can register themselves as capable of streaming every row in a table in one go via the new Response.stream() method. There are a couple of security fixes, one of which I deemed deserving of a GitHub advisory : private stored queries could be exposed, granting access to the title and SQL of the query (but not allowing that query to be executed). There are dozens of smaller improvements. The row page JSON representation finally has a design suitable for 1.0 . A new <datasette-copy-button> Web Component provides copy-schema in various places. JSON in columns on the row page can be pretty-printed. There's a new DatasetteModal.confirm() JavaScript utility method. Plus dozens of bug fixes, including contributions by Zihan Dai , Peter Olkhovets , Ilya Khalafi , and Ankita Advitot . The feature I'm most excited about is a pretty tiny one: I've added CSS multi-page view transitions to Datasette! Here's the commit - key CSS is as follows: /* Enable cross-document view transitions, for anyone without prefers-reduced-motion */ @media ( prefers-reduced-motion : no-preference ) { @view-transition { navigation : auto ; } } /* .facet-results should morph from old position to new */ html : active-view-transition . content > . facet-results { view-transition-name : facet-results ; } /* So should a .table-wrapper, provided it contains .rows-and-columns */ html : active-view-transition . table-wrapper : has ( > table . rows-and-columns ) { view-transition-name : rows-table ; } With that in place, navigations within Datasette - still staunchly a multi-page application - feel more like an SPA. This works on Safari and Chrome at the moment and I believe supports for Firefox is due to land in Firefox 162 on December 8th 2026 (seeing as they are no longer feature-flagged in Firefox Nightly.)
